newsitem.title: USA: Blue-chip stocks fall; small shares steady.
newsitem.headline: Blue-chip stocks fall; small shares steady.

text.p: Stock prices closed on a mixed note Thursday as investors took profits from the recent rally in blue chips and shifted to small-name shares, which have been lagging.
The Dow Jones industrial average closed down 32.56 points at 7,258.13.
The broader market showed some strength, with advancing issues leading declines 1,271 to 1,175 on active volume of 426 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.

The negative tone for blue chips came on the heels of a rally of more than 100 points earlier this week amid euphoria surrounding the Federal Reserve decision to keep interest rates unchanged after raising them a month earlier.
"We're been giving back some of the gains from that euphoric spike up," said said Scott Bleier, chief market strategist for Prime Charter Limited.
"But with the wild volatility in the market, which is here to stay, we need to digest gains in order to lessen the volatility above 7000," he said.
The Dow losses were also driven by weakness in bonds, with the yield on the benchmark 30-year bond rising briefly to the 7 percent level.
The benchmark 30-year Treasury bond fell 11/32, which raised its yield to 6.99 percent from Wednesday's 6.96 percent. Bond prices and yields move in opposite directions.
Analysts said the bond market was erratic as traders seemed confused after the Fed release the minutes from its March 25 policy-setting meeting.
The Fed panel voted 10-0 to move to a neutral monetary policy at the same time it raised rates.

The minutes, released with the customary six-week lag, painted a picture of a central bank increasingly worried about the risk of faster inflation but divided over how big a danger that posed to the economy.
"When negative comments were published from the minutes, bonds sold off. When positive comments came out, bonds came back," said Dick Stein, vice president at U.S. Clearing Corp.
Analysts said that the stocks of small-name companies and technology stocks held up nicely, thanks to the recent slump in the dollar, although it rebounded Thursday.

"Many technology companies easily make 50 percent or more of their revenues overseas, and they got killed earlier this year with the rise in interest rates and also because the dollar was so high," said Lary Aasheim, vice president at Philadelphia-based CoreStates Investment Advisers Inc.
The dollar rose to 116.10 Japanese yen from 114.35 at Wednesday's close. Dealers said volatility had decreased from the wide trading ranges seen earlier this week, but nerves remained raw.
Among individual stocks, Mail Boxes Etc. jumped 3 to 22-5/8 after U.S. Office Products said it was acquiring the company in a stock swap worth $276 million. U.S. Office was off 7/8 at 23-5/8.
Hartford Life Inc. jumped 3-7/8 to 32-1/8 in its initial public offering.
Two technology stocks were battered after warning of fiscal troubles. Canadian JetForm Corp. slumped 4-7/8 to 11 after it warned of disappointing quarterly profits.
CFM Technologies Inc. dropped 7-7/8 to 29-1/2 after it said aggressive pricing would hurt gross margins for the rest of its fiscal year.
Gateway, the 31st company to move from the Nasdaq to the NYSE so far this year, created a sensation by bringing a cow to the floor of the venerable exchange. It fell 3/4 to 68-1/2.
The Nasdaq Composite index slipped 1.16 points to 1,372.59.
The Standard & Poor's composite index of 500 stocks was off 3.69 to 835.66. The American Stock Exchange index rose 1.65 to 593.73.
The NYSE Composite index of all listed common stocks fell 1.55 to 434.66. The average share was down 15 cents.
The Wilshire Associates Equity Index -- the market value of NYSE, American and Nasdaq issues -- was 7,898.287 down 27.879 or 0.35 percent.
